what_it_does: When designing a microchip, engineers work from a high-level description (called RTL — a human-readable blueprint) down through a netlist (a detailed map of every logic gate and wire) to a physical layout on silicon. AI tools that try to assist with this design process need to understand netlists, but existing approaches rely on expensive simulation to teach the AI what gates do, and they only handle a simple subset of circuit types. NetTAG represents a netlist as a graph where each gate is a node carrying a text label — specifically the symbolic logic formula the gate computes plus physical properties — turning it into a text-attributed graph (hence the name). A large language model (an AI trained on text, like a scaled-up version of what powers chatbots) reads the gate formulas to understand logic semantics, while a graph transformer (an AI that processes relationships between nodes) captures how gates are wired together. The combined model is pre-trained with self-supervised objectives (no manual labels needed) and aligned to both the RTL blueprint stage and the physical layout stage, potentially enabling a single model to assist across the entire chip design flow. Details of performance gains are not available from the abstract.
